digest.intro: Thin day for hard news, thick day for things worth thinking about. A few genuine signals below.

items.title: Microsoft exec called AI scraping 'the largest theft of labor in human history'
items.blurb: Unredacted court filings reveal internal Microsoft fear of an AI 'doom loop' that kills news orgs and degrades the very training data future models depend on. The candor is more interesting than the claim.

items.title: ZCode, the GLM coding agent, silently uploads your Git history
items.blurb: Another AI coding tool caught exfiltrating data without disclosure. The pattern is becoming structural, not accidental — worth knowing which tools are in your environment.

items.title: Researchers used Claude to hack OpenAI
items.blurb: One frontier model used as an attack vector against a competitor's internal systems. The irony is almost too clean, but the security implication is real.

sections.heading: Language and what hides in it

items.title: Pre-Greek: The lost language hidden within Ancient Greek
items.blurb: Hundreds of Greek words — including names like Corinth and Olympus — come from a language spoken before Greeks arrived, now reconstructable only from residue. A genuine rabbit hole about what survives when a civilization is absorbed.

items.title: Bend 2 and the Vibe-Coding Trap
items.blurb: A sharp critique of using LLMs to build in a language specifically designed to prevent AI mistakes — the irony of vibe-coding your way past the proof system. Touches something real about what it means to understand your tools.

items.title: Through Carved Wooden Assemblages, Daniel Minter Communes with the Spiritual
items.blurb: "Do objects transmit spirituality? No, they remind us of our spirituality." Minter's carved assemblages as a practice of material thinking — the kind of work that makes you want to pick up a tool.

items.title: Cosmic amnesia — black holes ring like bells, then forget
items.blurb: A black hole struck by a merger rings like a bell, then settles into silence — losing almost all memory of what made it. An essay about information, entropy, and forgetting at the scale of spacetime.

art_picks.title: Jeanne Dielman, 23 Commerce Quay, 1080 Brussels
art_picks.creator: Chantal Akerman
art_picks.why: A film about invisible labor, ritual, and the brutal logic of systems hiding inside the domestic — the feedback loop between routine and selfhood made visible in real time. If you haven't sat with all 3h22m, now is the moment; if you have, it's one of those works that changes on every return.

art_picks.title: Black Sound / White Cube (and broader practice)
art_picks.creator: Theaster Gates
art_picks.why: Gates builds institutions disguised as art — record archives, renovation projects, community land trusts — using the aesthetics of craft and Black music as both material and argument. His work lives exactly at the edge where art functions as community infrastructure, and where beauty is a form of political organizing.

art_picks.title: Vespertine
art_picks.creator: Björk
art_picks.why: A record built entirely around the domestic micro-scale — breath, heartbeat, the creak of ice — rendered in generative electronics, harpsichord, and a 50-voice choir. It's a system for turning interior states into weather. The physical/digital boundary doesn't exist here; it was dissolved in the studio.

events.name: Sarah Michelson: nowhere
events.why: A live performance exhibition — not a show with a curtain but a durational, spatial presence running through the atrium over weeks — Michelson is one of the few choreographers who treats the architectural and social system of the gallery itself as the material.

events.name: Gaetano Pesce: A chair is a nest, is a foot, is a…
events.why: Pesce spent his career collapsing the boundary between object, body, and language — his furniture refuses to behave as furniture, which is the whole point; a tight gallery show of his work is a rare chance to be around objects that are genuinely trying to mean something.

events.name: Taryn Simon: Father Country I Do Love You
events.venue: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, 1071 Fifth Ave, Manhattan
events.why: Simon's first-ever fill of the entire Guggenheim rotunda — 42 interconnected works tracing one unnamed federal agent's life across photography, text, video, and sculpture, nearly a decade in the making; it's precisely about the invisible forces and hidden systems that shape national identity, and visitors choose their own path through the spiral.

events.name: Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony
events.why: The largest Jafa survey ever mounted — two full floors of his filmic collage practice, including Love is the Message, The Message is Death and The White Album, plus new work; his method of cutting archival footage, music video, and documentary material into 'affective proximities' is exactly the kind of unreasonably deep system-building in image-making that rewards close attention.

events.name: The Armory Show 2026
events.venue: Jacob K. Javits Convention Center, 429 11th Ave, Manhattan
events.why: 230+ galleries across four days, with the curated Focus and Platform sections centering Caribbean diaspora artists — worth it less for the blue-chip booths than for the Presents section's first-timers and the nonprofit floor, where the fair's actual social logic becomes legible.
